title: PAUL SAW WHAT HEAVEN WOULD NOT LET HIM TELL — AND THE REASON MAY CHANGE HOW YOU SEE YOUR SUFFERING FOREVER
paragraphs: PAUL SAW WHAT HEAVEN WOULD NOT LET HIM TELL — AND THE REASON MAY CHANGE HOW YOU SEE YOUR SUFFERING FOREVER

Why was the apostle Paul caught up to the third heaven, why was he forbidden to repeat what he heard, and why did God allow him to suffer afterward? The extraordinary truth of 2 Corinthians 12:1–10 reveals something far more important than a glimpse of paradise.
There are things you have begged God to show you.
Things you wanted Him to explain.

Why that prayer went unanswered. Why the person you loved walked away. Why the sickness remained. Why you tried to live faithfully, yet somehow found yourself crying in a room where nobody could hear you.
You have probably whispered it at least once.
“Lord, if You would just show me something. If You would just let me know You are really here.”
Now imagine being the apostle Paul.
Imagine being permitted to experience something so extraordinary that ordinary human language could not adequately describe it.
Imagine being caught up into paradise.
Hearing things no human being was permitted to repeat.
And then returning to a life where suffering had not disappeared.
Where enemies still opposed you.
Where your body could still hurt.
Where you could still plead with God for relief and hear an answer you never expected.
This happened to Paul.
But here is the part that should stop every Christian in their tracks.
Paul's greatest lesson did not come from what he saw in heaven. It came from what Christ taught him when the suffering remained.
And if you have ever wondered why God has not removed something you have prayed about for years, you need to hear the whole story.
Because this passage is not primarily an invitation to chase supernatural experiences.
It is an invitation to discover why the grace of Jesus Christ is sufficient even when your circumstances do not change.
Paul begins his account with words that almost seem reluctant.
“I knew a man in Christ above fourteen years ago…”
Then he adds something remarkable.
“Whether in the body, I cannot tell; or whether out of the body, I cannot tell: God knoweth…”
That is 2 Corinthians 12:2 in the King James Version.
Notice what Paul does not say.
He does not describe himself as a spiritual celebrity.
He does not announce that he has mastered the mysteries of heaven.
He does not even claim to know whether his experience involved his physical body.
Instead, he speaks of “a man in Christ,” referring indirectly to himself, as the surrounding context makes clear.
Why?
Because Paul is writing to a church struggling with spiritual pride, rival claims to authority, and teachers who measured greatness by outward impressiveness.
In the ancient world, people could gain attention by boasting about extraordinary religious experiences.
Paul had every opportunity to do the same.
Yet he handles this revelation with astonishing restraint.
He knows something many believers still struggle to understand.
An extraordinary spiritual experience does not make a person spiritually superior.
You can have a remarkable testimony and still need humility.
You can receive profound understanding and still need daily grace.
You can be used mightily by God and still be completely dependent on Jesus.
Then Paul reveals where this man was taken.
He was “caught up to the third heaven.”
The original Greek reads:
ἁρπαγέντα ἕως τρίτου οὐρανοῦ
harpagenta heōs tritou ouranou
Meaning: “having been caught up as far as the third heaven.”
The verb comes from harpazō, meaning to seize, snatch, or take away suddenly.
It describes something happening to Paul, not something Paul accomplished through his own spiritual ability.
He was caught up.
He did not climb there through meditation.
He did not unlock a secret heavenly doorway.
He did not discover a spiritual technique that ordinary Christians could reproduce.
God permitted the experience.
That distinction matters.
Because the moment we turn Paul's revelation into a formula for reaching heaven, we begin teaching something the passage never teaches.
And perhaps you are wondering what “third heaven” actually means.
To understand the expression, we must listen carefully to the biblical world in which Paul lived.
The Hebrew word for heaven is שָׁמַיִם (shamayim), a term used in Scripture for the heavens or sky, with its meaning determined by context.
Genesis 1:20 speaks of birds flying across the heavens.
Genesis 1:14–17 speaks of heavenly lights, including the sun, moon, and stars.
And passages such as 1 Kings 8:30 speak of heaven as God's dwelling place.
These passages show different biblical uses of the language of heaven.
Within a common traditional explanation, the first heaven refers to the atmospheric sky, the second to the starry heavens, and the third to God's heavenly dwelling.
This framework can help readers understand Paul's expression, although Scripture does not explicitly establish a numbered, three-level diagram of the universe.
Ancient Jewish writings also used varied descriptions of the heavens, so we should not pretend every ancient writer followed one identical system.
What we can say with confidence is that Paul immediately connects this extraordinary experience with paradise.
In 2 Corinthians 12:4, he writes that he was:
The Greek word translated “paradise” is παράδεισος (paradeisos).
The term has associations with a garden or enclosed park and was used in Jewish and Christian contexts for a place of blessedness.
It also appears in Luke 23:43, when Jesus tells the repentant criminal:
“Verily I say unto thee, To day shalt thou be with me in paradise.”
And it appears in Revelation 2:7, where Jesus promises the overcomer access to the tree of life in the paradise of God.
These connections are beautiful.
But do not miss what makes paradise truly glorious.
It is not merely the thought of streets of gold.
It is not simply freedom from sickness.
It is not even the reunion we long for with those who died in Christ.
The supreme joy of heaven is the presence of God and the fulfillment of His promises through Jesus Christ.
A place without pain would be wonderful.
But eternal life is more than the absence of pain.
Jesus says in John 17:3 that eternal life is knowing the only true God and Jesus Christ whom He sent.
Heaven is glorious because God is glorious.
And Paul was granted an extraordinary experience of heavenly reality.
Yet there is a detail that should humble every person who claims to know exactly what heaven looks like.
Paul does not tell us what he saw.
He tells us that he heard things he was not permitted to repeat.
The Greek expression is:
ἄρρητα ῥήματα
arrēta rhēmata
Words that are unutterable, or words not to be spoken.
Paul adds that these were things:
οὐκ ἐξὸν ἀνθρώπῳ λαλῆσαι
ouk exon anthrōpō lalēsai
Meaning that it is not permitted for a human being to speak them.
The passage does not tell us the specific content of those words.
It does not reveal the conversations Paul heard.
It does not give us a heavenly travel itinerary.
And that silence is part of the lesson.
Because Paul, who had received an extraordinary revelation, refused to build his ministry around disclosing what God had not authorized him to disclose.
Think about that.
Some people today would turn a mysterious experience into an entire platform.
A book.
A tour.
A promise that you, too, can discover the hidden secrets of heaven.
But Paul does something almost unimaginable in a culture obsessed with spectacle.
He refuses to exploit the mystery.
He points away from himself.
And when you continue reading, you discover why.
Because the story does not end in paradise.
It continues with pain.
Paul writes in 2 Corinthians 12:7:
Read those words slowly.
The man who had been caught up to the third heaven was also afflicted by a thorn in the flesh.
The man who had received extraordinary revelations still experienced deep personal weakness.
The man who could speak of paradise could also speak of suffering.
Paul does not identify the thorn precisely.
Some interpreters have suggested a physical illness. Others have proposed persecution, spiritual opposition, or another persistent affliction.
But Scripture does not give enough information to identify it with certainty.
We should not claim to know what God has chosen not to specify.
What Paul does tell us is that this affliction was deeply distressing and that God used it to prevent him from becoming conceited.
Paul calls it a messenger of Satan, while also recognizing God's sovereign purpose in permitting the trial.
This does not mean that suffering is automatically evidence of God's punishment.
It does not mean every illness is caused by a demon.
And it certainly does not mean that every person suffering is secretly proud.
Paul is describing his own experience and the purpose Christ revealed to him.
But his testimony teaches a truth that reaches far beyond his circumstances.
A person can be deeply loved by God and still suffer deeply.
Somebody reading this needs that sentence.
Because somewhere along the way, you may have begun believing that if God truly loved you, life would be easier.
That if your faith were strong enough, the pain would disappear.
That if you prayed correctly, the answer would always be immediate deliverance.
But look at Paul.
He loved Christ.
He served Christ.
He endured hardship for Christ.
And still, he had a thorn.
Not because Jesus had abandoned him.
Not because the Gospel had failed.
Not because his prayers were meaningless.
His suffering remained within the mysterious providence of God, and Christ would teach him something through it.
Paul says he pleaded with the Lord three times for the thorn to depart.
Three times.
This was not a man pretending his pain did not hurt.
He wanted relief.
He asked for it.
And there is something profoundly comforting about that.
You do not have to pretend you are comfortable with suffering to be faithful to Jesus.
You can cry.
You can ask for healing.
You can tell God that you are tired.
You can pray again about the burden you have carried for years.
Biblical faith is not the denial of pain.
It is bringing your pain honestly before the Lord.
But then comes the answer that changes the entire passage.
Jesus tells Paul:
“My grace is sufficient for thee: for my strength is made perfect in weakness.”
— 2 Corinthians 12:9, KJV
In Greek, the opening declaration reads:
Ἀρκεῖ σοι ἡ χάρις μου
Arkei soi hē charis mou
“My grace is sufficient for you.”
The verb arkei expresses sufficiency: being enough, meeting what is needed.
The word charis means grace, here referring to the sustaining favor and help of Christ.
Notice what Jesus does not promise Paul.
He does not promise that the thorn will disappear that night.
He does not tell Paul that stronger faith will make suffering impossible.
He does not suggest that the apostle has somehow failed because he needs help.
Instead, Christ promises something greater than self-sufficiency.
His own grace.
His own strength.
His own sustaining presence.
And suddenly the third heaven becomes part of a much larger story.
Paul had experienced an extraordinary revelation of heavenly glory.
But the Lord was teaching him to depend on Christ in ordinary human weakness.
The revelation was real.
The suffering was real.
And the grace was real.
Maybe that is where this story begins touching your own life.
Because you may never experience what Paul experienced.
You may never receive a vision of paradise.
You may never hear mysteries beyond human permission to repeat.
But if you belong to Jesus Christ, you have access to the same Savior whose grace sustained Paul.
Not because your suffering is identical to his.
Not because every unanswered prayer has the same explanation.
But because the Christ who spoke to Paul remains faithful to His people.
And perhaps the question you have been asking needs to change.
You have been asking, “Lord, why have You not taken this away?”
That is an honest question.
Keep bringing it to Him.
But alongside it, perhaps you can begin asking:
“Lord, how can I trust You here?”
“How can Your strength sustain me when mine is failing?”
“How can I remain faithful even before I understand?”
Because the deepest lesson of Paul's third-heaven experience is not that Christians should seek extraordinary revelations.
It is that even extraordinary revelations cannot replace our daily need for Christ.
Paul eventually says:
“Most gladly therefore will I rather glory in my infirmities, that the power of Christ may rest upon me.”
He is not celebrating pain for its own sake.
He is rejoicing that weakness does not disqualify him from receiving the sustaining power of Christ.
That is a radically different understanding of spiritual strength.
We live in a world that tells us to hide our weaknesses.
Hide the tears.
Hide the struggle.
Hide the failures.
Make everybody believe you are doing well.
And sometimes even Christian communities unintentionally reinforce that pressure.
We know how to say, “God is good.”
But we do not always know how to say, “I am hurting, and I need someone to pray with me.”
We know how to post the testimony after the breakthrough.
But we are often afraid to admit that the breakthrough has not come.
Paul shows us another way.
He does not glorify himself.
He glorifies the sufficiency of Christ.
And here is where this passage becomes even more powerful.
The same apostle who spoke about being caught up to the third heaven also preached a Savior who came down from heaven to rescue sinners.
Jesus Christ did not merely reveal heavenly truth from a distance.
The eternal Son of God took on human flesh.
He entered a world of rejection, suffering, betrayal, and death.
He was despised.
He was mocked.
He was crucified.
And unlike Paul, who was granted an extraordinary glimpse of heavenly glory, Jesus willingly endured the shame of the cross to accomplish our redemption.
He did not die because He was powerless.
He gave Himself for sinners.
He bore our sins, died, was buried, and rose again, as the apostolic Gospel declares in 1 Corinthians 15:3–4.
This is why Christianity is not ultimately about chasing visions.
It is about knowing the crucified and risen Lord.
It is about repentance and forgiveness.
It is about grace that reaches guilty people who could never save themselves.
It is about sinners becoming new creations through Jesus Christ.
And perhaps you know something about needing that grace.
Maybe you have made choices you still regret.
Maybe there are chapters of your life you wish nobody could read.
Maybe you have lived behind a carefully maintained Christian appearance while privately struggling with bitterness, lust, envy, dishonesty, pride, or unbelief.
Maybe you have wandered so far that returning to God feels embarrassing.
But listen carefully.
The Gospel does not say you can erase your own past.
It says Jesus Christ is mighty to save.
The cross does not pretend sin is harmless.
It reveals how serious sin is and how astonishing God's mercy truly is.
And the resurrection declares that sin and death do not have the final word over those who belong to Christ.
That is why our message is:
Not because Jesus makes the consequences of every past decision vanish.
Not because repentance guarantees an easy life.
Not because every broken relationship will be restored exactly as we desire.
But because the risen Christ forgives sinners, reconciles believers to God, gives new life, and begins a transformation that will one day be completed in glory.
Paul knew that transformation personally.
Before becoming an apostle, he persecuted the church.
He approved of violence against followers of Jesus.
He carried a history that could never be described as harmless.
Yet the grace of God met him.
The persecutor became a preacher of the Gospel.
The enemy of the church became its servant.
And the man who once opposed the name of Jesus would eventually declare that Christ's grace was sufficient for him.
Do you see the beauty?
The greatest miracle in Paul's life was not merely that he was caught up to the third heaven.
It was that the risen Jesus had saved him.
And the greatest miracle available to you is not a supernatural tour of paradise.
It is reconciliation with God through Jesus Christ.
You do not need to know the secret words Paul heard in heaven to know the Gospel God has already revealed in Scripture.
You do not need a heavenly vision to know that Jesus died for sinners and rose again.
You do not need to become spiritually impressive before coming to Christ.
You need His mercy.
And His invitation is not limited to people with clean histories.
It extends to sinners who repent and believe.
Perhaps you have been reading this with tears in your eyes.
Perhaps nobody knows how exhausted you have become.
Perhaps you are the person everybody calls strong, while privately wondering how much longer you can keep going.
Hear this.
Your weakness does not place you beyond the reach of Jesus.
Your unanswered questions do not surprise Him.
Your tears are not proof that your faith is worthless.
And your past does not have to define your future if you turn to Christ.
That does not mean you should carry every burden alone. Seek prayer, wise pastoral care, and practical help when you need them.
God often strengthens His people through the love and care of others.
But above every human support stands the promise of Christ.
“My grace is sufficient for thee.”
Not your perfection.
Not your reputation.
Not your ability to appear strong.
His grace.
And that is where Paul's story brings us.
Not to a map of heaven.
Not to a collection of forbidden mysteries.
But to Jesus.
The One whose strength is made perfect in weakness.
The One who receives repentant sinners.
The One who transforms lives that once seemed beyond redemption.
The One who promises eternal life to those who believe in Him.
And one day, those who belong to Christ will not need to speculate about the glory awaiting them.
They will be with the Lord.
Until then, we walk by faith, not by sight.
We hold fast to what God has revealed.
We endure by His grace.
And we continue looking to Jesus.
Not as a formula for receiving a miracle, but as an honest expression of your need for God and the encouragement of fellow believers.
Your experience may help another believer feel less alone and encourage them to turn to Scripture and prayer.
Someone on your Facebook friends list may be silently wrestling with the same questions.
Someone may be convinced that God has abandoned them because their prayers remain unanswered.
Someone may have mistaken suffering for evidence that Jesus no longer cares.
Because the world has no shortage of voices promising shortcuts to glory.
What we need is more people faithfully pointing to Jesus.
That is also why we are continuing to build and expand Gospel Warrior as a place for biblical nourishment and discipleship.
We want these resources to remain accessible to people who may not have the means to purchase Christian books or discipleship materials.
Scripture teaches in 2 Corinthians 9:7 that giving should not come from reluctance or compulsion, because God loves a cheerful giver.
Your first responsibility is faithfulness to Christ, not financial loyalty to any online ministry.
And if you are already faithfully supporting your local church, caring for your family, or facing financial hardship, please do not feel pressured to give beyond your means.
You can still support the spread of the Gospel through prayer, encouragement, sharing these articles, and helping others discover the free resources.
That Jesus Christ would be glorified.
That the Gospel would be understood.
That sinners would find forgiveness through repentance and faith.
That wounded believers would find encouragement in the promises of God.
And that more people would discover that the grace of Christ is not merely a beautiful religious phrase.
It is the sustaining gift of the Savior who died and rose again.
Now return to Paul for one final moment.
He was caught up to the third heaven.
He heard what he could not repeat.
He experienced something most of us can scarcely imagine.
Yet when he wanted believers to understand the strength that sustained him, he did not give them the secret words of paradise.
He gave them the words of Jesus.
“My grace is sufficient for thee.”
Maybe that is the message you needed today.
Not a promise that every thorn will be removed.
Not an explanation for every unanswered prayer.
But the assurance that your suffering does not have to separate you from the Savior.
Because the One who holds the glory of heaven is also the One who meets His people in their weakness.
Paul was caught up to heaven and returned with words he could not repeat—but in his weakness, Christ gave him words the whole world needed to hear: “My grace is sufficient for thee.”
